Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I worked as a civil servant at a government institute in my home country. I have a wife and five children. I fear my wife's sister's husband, who committed domestic violence and heads a powerful family of warlords in the north of my home country.

In 2014, he approached me at a family wedding and asked me to give my fourteen-year-old daughter in marriage to his son. I was reluctant to discuss the proposal and told him that my daughter needed an education. He threatened me at gunpoint and publicly announced that my daughter would be his son's future wife. This created a dispute over family honour.

The next day, I hired a car and fled with my family to the capital, 420 kilometres from our home. My wife and five children hid at a friend's residence. I continued working at a government office and slept in a secure dormitory within a work compound. While I was staying in the capital, I learned that my wife's brother-in-law had approached family members to find us.

I applied for a passport in 2014 and received a United States visa in 2015. My supervisor arranged for me to attend a conference in the United States. I left my home country in 2015, while my wife and children remained with our friend.

On February 23, 2015, I attempted to enter Canada at Niagara Falls to seek refugee protection. I could not enter because my uncle was outside Canada and could not verify our relationship. I returned to the United States and stayed with relatives in the Boston area. On July 20, 2015, I went to the Peace Bridge, where my uncle met me, and made a refugee claim in Canada. I still fear my wife's brother-in-law.

Testimony of Henrik Dahl

My name is Henrik Dahl. I am a gay man with effeminate mannerisms. In my home country, I did not tell anyone that I was gay, and I kept my relationship with my boyfriend private. We began our relationship in 2006. It was my first serious relationship.

At school, people ridiculed and mocked me because of my mannerisms. My family and neighbours challenged how I behaved. People asked where my girlfriend was and told me that I was not behaving as a man. My cousins were involved in assaults against me, including incidents when I was thirteen. I also experienced an assault later in my life. I have a desire to dress as a woman.

My boyfriend's father discovered our relationship in 2006 and became infuriated. That year, two police officers assaulted me. They struck me and told me to stay away from my boyfriend. The next day, I went to the police station to make a formal complaint. I saw one of the officers who had attacked me there. I went home and decided not to pursue the complaint.

I lost my job and left my hometown to stay with relatives in another city. My family back home received threatening notes and drawings. My cousins who valued masculine behaviour were angry with me.

I arrived in Canada on January 10, 2007, and requested refugee protection on February 6, 2007. I fear being killed by my boyfriend's father, the police, or homophobic members of my community, including my cousins. My fear extends beyond my hometown to other parts of my home country.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a citizen of my home country and the mother of a 16-year-old son. My son and I are Sunni Muslims. I moved to another country at an early age because my father worked there. I met my husband there. He is also a citizen of my home country, and our son was born in the country where we lived.

My husband remains there. We do not have permanent immigration status there. The government gives temporary visas to people working in the country. My husband lost his job in 2015, and we were required to leave in 2016. We could not remain there permanently on the basis of our residence.

My husband has not returned to my home country since 1981. The authorities attribute political opinions to him, and I fear persecution because I am his wife. I visited my home country in 2002 and 2010. During those visits, I was questioned about my husband. I have not returned since 2010.

I fear imprisonment and torture if I return, particularly in the context of the civil war. My religious identity increases my fear because much of the opposition shares that identity.

I also fear that my son will be recruited into the army and killed. My son and I oppose the government. We regard it as responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity, and he does not want to participate in those acts.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am of mixed ancestry, with one half belonging to an ethnic minority in my home country. My husband belongs to the majority population. We have a son.

I experienced discrimination in housing, at work, and in education because of my ethnic background. I finished school and worked from 1999 to 2009. I lived and worked in damp conditions, which caused me to develop a disease. When I was not working, I received child benefits and health benefits because of my medical condition. My mother and brother also received government benefits.

My family experienced two assaults by skinheads, one in 2001 and another in 2009. In 2001, unknown individuals approached us in the street. My husband was assaulted and received medical attention. The assault was reported to the police.

In 2009, I was attacked in the dark while vomiting behind some bushes. I reported this assault to the police. I did not follow up with them after making my report because I left for Canada. We did not seek assistance from anyone other than the police.

The 2009 attack prompted us to leave my home country. My husband, our son, and I came to Canada and sought refugee protection in 2009. I fear returning because we could face further attacks, and I do not expect the police to protect us if we encounter more problems.

Testimony of Martin Lund

My name is Martin Lund. My parents have different ethnic origins, and my mother belongs to an ethnic minority in my home country. I publicly denounced discrimination and tensions between people of different ethnic backgrounds. I was assaulted three times after addressing groups of people from that minority in my hometown: once in 2009 and twice in 2010.

During each assault, eight to ten people attacked and beat me before running away. My attackers were members of an extremist nationalist group. Two assaults followed demonstrations organized by Second World War veterans, most of whom belonged to the minority community, commemorating their wartime victory. Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I fear persecution in my home country because of my affiliation with an opposition party. I fear the ruling party's youth members and the authorities.

In 2000, my neighbour warned me that I was suspected of belonging to the opposition party. Two men wearing dark glasses came to my house and ransacked it. They accused me of supporting the opposition party's secretary general. They manhandled me and confiscated opposition pamphlets, T-shirts and my party membership card. They demanded the identities of other party members. I was terrified and gave them false names and addresses. I fled to my mother's house.

A short time later, strangers came to my workplace and accused me of working for a White-owned firm. After this incident, I stopped working and stayed at my mother's house until I left my home country.

I entered the United States in 2000 without my children. My husband brought our children to the United States later that year, and we were reunited. My husband and I separated in 2002, and he returned to my home country.

In 2003, my mother told me that people had come to her house looking for me. When she could not produce me, they threatened to abduct her and take her to prison. This frightened me.

In 2004, my brother returned from the United States. He was imprisoned and beaten because of his affiliation with the opposition party, and his finger was dislocated. His political activities were similar to mine. My mother told me what had happened just after his release, before he went into hiding.

My children and I entered Canada in 2005 and sought protection. I fear that I will be harmed if I return because of my political affiliation.

I fear arrest and detention for violating police policy and remaining abroad beyond my authorized stay. I fear more severe treatment because I am a dismissed police officer. Authorities may suspect that I have been working in Canada against the ruling party. I fear that those questioning me will reject my explanation for my time abroad, accuse me of revealing state secrets to Western countries, and torture me to obtain a confession.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. After completing studies in the United States, I returned to my home country and resumed my career. While working at a school, I witnessed drug activities and reported them according to the school's policy. The police were called, and their investigation led to a gang.

Through an intermediary, I received a warning that the gang knew I had caused the police to become involved. They said that unless I ignored future drug activities at the school, I would leave in a body bag. I reported the threats to the police. They told me there was little they could do because it was one person's word against another's.

A few days later, I was involved in a serious road accident. My vehicle ran off the road because unknown people had loosened the lug nuts on both front tires. The police questioned a suspect, who said he had not been on the island that day. They did not follow up.

Fearing for my life, I requested a transfer, which was granted in 2004. In 2007, at my new school, I saw boys entering a vacant campus building. I investigated and discovered students trafficking marijuana. I took the students to the principal's office, and the police were called. The drugs were traced to the same gang.

Within three weeks, I learned that two men were looking for me and that the gang leader had sent two armed men to get me. I kept a low profile until the academic year ended, then travelled to Canada for a vacation to escape the threats. While I was there, a friend from my home country warned me that my life remained in danger. Police raids were continuing, and the gang blamed me in part for them. I sought protection in Canada because I feared the gang would kill me if I returned.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. My brother and I left my home country because another family threatened to kill members of our family in revenge for a death. My parents and two sisters remain there.

In 2009, two burglars broke into our family’s business and home. My father shot one of them in self-defense. He called the police, and the injured man was taken to hospital, where he died. My father was prosecuted and later found not guilty.

The dead man’s family sent an envoy to tell us that they had declared a blood feud against our family. We stayed inside our home to protect ourselves from revenge killings. My father remained confined to the house. After one week at home, the girls resumed attending school with my uncle accompanying them. My mother went out for groceries and sometimes accompanied the girls to school. She also had someone accompany her.

My sisters were followed outside the house. My uncle called the police, who patrolled the area along their route to school. People also came at night and banged and kicked the downstairs doors. When we complained, the police came and patrolled the area. They patrolled our house for six months during my father’s house arrest and also came when we requested help. These patrols did not end the threats.

My father sought help through his connections and contacted a nationwide reconciliation organization, but the other family refused reconciliation. Moving elsewhere in my home country would not protect us because the country is small. We know people who tried moving and were killed.

My brother and I obtained Canadian visas for summer camp without an interview, through the Canadian embassy in Rome. We travelled to Canada, requested protection, and stayed. I fear returning because the other family has sworn revenge against us.

Testimony of Erik Johansson

My name is Erik Johansson. I was born in a part of my home country controlled by an armed group. In 1990, my family moved to a nearby town controlled by the army.

In 1998, security forces apprehended me because they suspected that I had connections to the armed group because of my birthplace. They separated the people they had apprehended into men and women, then placed me in a group of fifteen young men. They interrogated us individually and tortured me. I was threatened and beaten. My school principal intervened, and I was released that year.

In 2000, my family moved to another town. I attended school and looked for work. Members of the armed group often came to our home at night demanding food and money and trying to recruit young people. I stopped attending school in 2003 because of their ongoing harassment. In 2004, I started a business. Security officers frequently stopped me and questioned me about connections to the armed group.

In 2009, security forces took me to a police station and detained, interrogated, threatened, and beat me. My father arranged my release by paying a large sum through a friend. My uncle then arranged for an agent to help me leave the country. While I waited in the capital, police raided the place where I was staying and ordered me to return home. I nevertheless left in 2009.

I flew through Thailand to Mexico and entered the United States illegally in 2009. I was arrested and detained until 2010. I made an asylum claim there but abandoned it after my release. I travelled to Canada and claimed refugee protection on February 9, 2010.

I fear arrest if I return because authorities have arrested me twice and would again suspect me of association with the armed group. I also fear extortion by a paramilitary group that has extorted my family because of my situation.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am 48 years old. I operated a shop in my hometown. I bought goods in the capital and transported them to my hometown to sell. The bags carried my name so that they could be identified during transportation.

In 2000, rebels from neighbouring countries raided my shop and stole my bags. There was fighting between the army and the rebels in the area. I feared for my life and moved back to the capital.

In 2001, the army arrested and imprisoned me while searching for people accused of helping the rebels. Soldiers had seized bags bearing my name. They accused me of supplying rice to the rebels who had entered my home country to destabilize it.

I spent six months in prison. During that time, I was subjected to intense interrogation. My elbows were tied together with rope. I was beaten and forced to kneel in the sun against a wall. I was flogged on my hips four times a day to make me reveal my ties with the rebels. I denied having those ties, and the more I denied the accusations, the harder they tortured me.

My friends helped me escape. I hid for two months and then left my home country with a Canadian visa.

The security forces are still looking for me. If I return, I fear they will arrest, imprison and torture me again to force me to admit helping the rebels and identify other people they assume I know. I fear dying from that torture.

Testimony of Martin Lund

My name is Martin Lund. I am an 18-year-old man from my home country and a recent high school graduate. I belong to an ethnic minority and actively supported an opposition political party. I participated in political demonstrations.

Beginning in 2013, police detained me twice because of my involvement in demonstrations. During both detentions, they mistreated me. The police continued to target me after my initial arrests.

My mother helped me obtain a visa to travel to Canada in 2014. I did not leave immediately after receiving the visa. Both my mother and I were experiencing psychological difficulties because of what we had gone through, and I did not want to leave her. After another police raid in 2014, my mother and I decided that I should leave. We made the arrangements, and I departed my home country that year.

This was my first journey outside my home country. I travelled to Canada and filed my refugee protection claim in August 2014. The police have continued looking for me since my departure. I fear returning because they detained and mistreated me for my political activities, repeatedly came to my home, and beat and threatened me there.

Testimony of Henrik Dahl

My name is Henrik Dahl. I was born in 1980, and my wife was born in 1984. We lived in my home country. I opposed the former regime, but I did not take an active part in the uprising or the revolution.

In 2011, armed groups came looking for me because of a friend who was involved in the uprising. My name became associated with the uprising through that connection. I had to hide temporarily.

In 2012, I experienced problems at work. A neighbour associated with a militia group also caused problems for me. In 2013, threats against me forced me to leave my neighbourhood.

I tried to leave my home country and escape the situation. The conflict and difficulties obtaining permission to travel to another country delayed my departure. I secured a Canadian visa in 2014 and left my home country that year. In 2014, I learned that militia forces had occupied my home.

In 2015, I decided to stay in Canada because I realized that returning would not be safe. My daughter was born that year, and I could not immediately concentrate on making a protection claim. I claimed protection in December 2015.

I fear the armed groups operating in the area where I lived. I could be targeted because of where I lived and my association with a particular tribe. I also oppose the hardline armed groups operating in my home country and fear returning while these groups are active.

Testimony of Jonas Lindqvist

My name is Jonas Lindqvist. My family and I lived in an area of my home country controlled by an armed group. Fighting displaced us several times, and we fled from village to village.

The armed group harassed and beat my family to force them to hand over my brother. He was hiding, and my parents refused to surrender him. My sister and I found my brother and told him what was happening. He turned himself in to save our parents. He was subsequently killed in fighting.

In 2009, the army took all the residents of our area to a camp and registered us. After several months, officers from the criminal investigation department demanded money. I refused their first demand. They took me away and held me for two days until my mother paid them. They came twice more to demand money. My family feared that they would kidnap me because we could not pay.

My family bribed an army officer so that I could have my photograph taken for a passport. My father found an agent who would obtain a passport for me. In 2009, I escaped from the camp and got a ride to another place, where I found the agent. He helped me board a train to the capital.

I feared arrest, so I flew to Thailand. Another agent arranged my lodgings there. Later in 2009, I boarded a ship bound for Canada. I arrived on October 17, 2009, and sought refugee protection.

I fear that the army, criminal investigation officers, and the armed group will harm me if I return because I escaped from the camp and because I am a young man from a minority ethnic group. I also fear returning because of the widespread media coverage of the ship on which I travelled.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I grew up in a town in my home country that an armed group controlled from 1990 to 1995. When the army captured the town in 1995, I fled with my family to another area and worked on my father's farm. The armed group controlled that area and conscripted young men from my ethnic minority, particularly unmarried men. I married to avoid conscription. In 2000, my family obtained a pass to move elsewhere.

Army members frequently harassed me at checkpoints. After hearing that members of my ethnic minority had been killed, I arranged through an agent to travel to Malaysia. The agent promised to help me find work but did not, so I returned to my home country. I then tried to fly from the capital to Singapore, but I lacked the money to pay a bribe to leave and returned home.

At one checkpoint, soldiers threatened me because my identity card showed where I came from. They released me only after my wife and father-in-law pleaded for my release. I later obtained a new identity card showing my current address.

I visited my sister after her daughter was injured in a raid. I tried to obtain passes for us to leave, but the armed group refused. In 2009, we went to a displaced persons camp and then fled to an army-controlled area. I was separated from my sister's family, interrogated, tortured, and hospitalized. My wife and her brother sneaked me out of the hospital. I stayed with her brother rather than at home. Army intelligence agents repeatedly visited my home and told my wife I would be shot for escaping.

I left for Thailand and registered with UNHCR. In April 2010, I boarded a ship bound for Canada, arriving on August 13, 2010. From a detention centre, I telephoned my wife and learned that criminal investigators had questioned her several times. I fear returning because of the torture and threats against me.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

This testimony was given through a Somali interpreter.

My name is Peter Hansen. I grew up in a town in my home country that an armed group controlled from 1990 to 1995. When the army captured the town in 1995, I fled with my family to another area and worked on my father's farm. The armed group controlled that area and conscripted young men from my ethnic minority, particularly unmarried men. I married to avoid conscription. In 2000, my family obtained a pass to move elsewhere.

Army members frequently harassed me at checkpoints. After hearing that members of my ethnic minority had been killed, I arranged through an agent to travel to Malaysia. The agent promised to help me find work but did not, so I returned to my home country. I then tried to fly from the capital to Singapore, but I lacked the money to pay a bribe to leave and returned home.

At one checkpoint, soldiers threatened me because my identity card showed where I came from. They released me only after my wife and father-in-law pleaded for my release. I later obtained a new identity card showing my current address.

I visited my sister after her daughter was injured in a raid. I tried to obtain passes for us to leave, but the armed group refused. In 2009, we went to a displaced persons camp and then fled to an army-controlled area. I was separated from my sister's family, interrogated, tortured, and hospitalized. My wife and her brother sneaked me out of the hospital. I stayed with her brother rather than at home. Army intelligence agents repeatedly visited my home and told my wife I would be shot for escaping.
